title: “GOD TOLD ME TO MARRY SOMEONE ELSE.” — WHEN YOUR SPOUSE USES GOD’S NAME TO BREAK YOUR HEART
paragraphs: “GOD TOLD ME TO MARRY SOMEONE ELSE.” — WHEN YOUR SPOUSE USES GOD’S NAME TO BREAK YOUR HEART

What do you do when the person who promised you forever suddenly claims heaven has chosen someone else? Before you beg them to stay, blame yourself, or question your faith, there is something Jesus wants you to understand about covenant, betrayal, spiritual deception, and the grace that can meet you in the wreckage.
There are sentences that hurt.
And then there are sentences that change the way you hear someone's voice forever.
“I don't love you anymore.”
“I've met someone else.”
“I think we made a mistake.”

But imagine sitting across from the person you married. The person whose hand you held before God. The person you prayed with, built a home with, perhaps raised children with. The person who once looked into your eyes and promised to remain faithful through sickness, poverty, hardship, and everything life could throw at you.
And now that same person looks at you with an unsettling calm and says:
“God told me you're not the one anymore. He told me I'm supposed to marry someone else.”
For a moment, the room becomes painfully quiet.
You can hear your own breathing.
Your mind races backward through years of memories, arguments, sacrifices, forgiveness, anniversaries, and whispered prayers.
Was I not enough?
Did I fail as a husband?
Did I fail as a wife?
Was our marriage a mistake?
And perhaps the most devastating question of all:
“God, did You really tell the person I love to abandon me?”
If you've ever heard anything remotely like this, I want you to keep reading.
Somewhere in your family, church, workplace, or circle of friends, someone may be suffering beneath a sentence that sounds spiritual but is tearing their life apart.
Because the issue here is bigger than an unfaithful spouse.
It is about what happens when someone attaches God's holy name to a decision that must be tested against God's written Word.
And before we reach the end, we need to confront a truth that may disturb both the person who wants to leave and the person desperately trying to make them stay.
God's Word must judge our claimed revelations. Our claimed revelations do not get to rewrite God's Word.
The Bible gives us a sobering picture of marriage in Malachi 2:14.
The prophet speaks of the wife of a man's youth, calling her his companion and his wife by covenant.
The Hebrew word translated “covenant” is בְּרִית (berit).
It carries the idea of a binding covenantal relationship, not merely a passing emotional preference.
And the Hebrew expression אֵשֶׁת בְּרִיתֶךָ (eshet beritek) means “the wife of your covenant.”
Think about that.
Not simply the woman who makes you happy.
Not merely the person who currently satisfies your emotional needs.
Not someone whose place can automatically be given to another when the excitement fades.
Your covenant partner.

Malachi's rebuke was directed particularly at men who were dealing faithlessly with their wives. Its original context matters. It was not a command for victims to endure every kind of mistreatment without protection. It was a prophetic confrontation of covenant betrayal.
And that confrontation still has something urgent to say to anyone who believes a new romantic attraction gives them divine permission to discard their spouse.
Jesus made the covenantal seriousness of marriage even clearer.
In Matthew 19:6, He declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” (KJV)
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say marriage remains sacred only while both people feel butterflies.
He did not say a covenant expires when someone more attractive, more attentive, more exciting, or seemingly more spiritually compatible appears.
He called people to honor what God has joined.
Now imagine someone saying:
“I know I made vows before God. But I've been praying, and I have peace about leaving you for someone else.”
That sounds convincing to people who have never learned to distinguish spiritual discernment from emotional desire.
But peace alone is not proof of divine approval.

A person can feel relief after making a selfish decision. A person can feel excited about something destructive. A person can mistake the disappearance of inner conflict for the presence of God's blessing.
Not every feeling of peace is the peace of Christ.
This is why Scripture tells believers to test spiritual claims.
First John 4:1 says:
“Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God.” (KJV)
The Greek phrase δοκιμάζετε τὰ πνεύματα (dokimazete ta pneumata) means “test the spirits.”
The verb dokimazete carries the sense of examining or evaluating to determine genuineness.
In its immediate context, John was warning believers about false prophets and their teaching concerning Jesus Christ. We should not pretend the verse was written specifically about marital disputes.
But its call to discernment establishes an important principle: a spiritual-sounding claim is not automatically trustworthy simply because someone says it came from God.
So when a spouse says, “God told me to marry someone else,” the biblical response is not to surrender your discernment.
It is to ask:
“How does that claim agree with what God has already revealed in Scripture?”

And if that supposed revelation is being used to justify adultery, deception, abandonment, or the pursuit of another person while an existing marriage covenant remains in place, it must be rejected as divine authorization.
Hebrews 13:4 says:
“Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge.” (KJV)
The Greek word μοιχούς (moichous) refers to adulterers.
There is no hidden Greek exception that says adultery becomes holy when someone calls the new relationship a prophetic assignment.
No secret biblical passage says a marriage covenant can be exchanged for a supposedly more anointed partner.
No apostle taught that spiritual compatibility with a third person gives someone permission to betray the spouse they already have.
And this is where things become deeply uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the statement “God told me” is not the beginning of a revelation.
Sometimes it is the final stage of an attachment that should never have been cultivated.
It may have begun with innocent-looking messages.
Then private conversations.
Then emotional dependence.
Then comparing a spouse's weaknesses with someone else's strengths.
Then imagining what life might look like with that other person.
Then prayer—not necessarily to seek God's will with an open heart, but perhaps to find permission for a desire that has already taken root.
We cannot know another person's motives merely from their words. Not every troubled marriage involves an affair, and not every person who claims divine guidance is deliberately lying.
But when someone has already formed a romantic attachment outside marriage, that attachment cannot be treated as neutral evidence that God wants a different spouse.
James 1:14 warns that a person can be drawn away by their own desire.
The Greek word ἐπιθυμίας (epithymias) refers to desire or longing; in this context, desire that entices toward sin.
Desire itself must be understood in context. The word is not always negative throughout the New Testament. But James is specifically describing the progression of temptation toward sin and death.
And that matters because a powerful desire is not the same thing as a divine direction.
You can want something desperately and still be wrong to pursue it.
You can feel understood by another person and still be responsible for honoring your vows.
You can experience problems in your marriage without having biblical permission to begin another romantic relationship.
And you can sincerely believe God is speaking while profoundly misunderstanding what He requires.
But now I want to speak directly to the spouse who has been left trembling by those words.
The one who has cried in the bathroom so the children wouldn't hear.
The one who still checks the phone, hoping for a message that says, “I'm sorry. I was wrong.”

The one who lies awake wondering whether they should become more attractive, more submissive, more successful, more affectionate, more spiritual—anything that might make their spouse choose them again.
Please hear this.
Someone else's decision to betray their vows is not proof that you are unworthy of love.
It is possible that your marriage has real problems.
Perhaps there have been years of unresolved conflict, neglect, poor communication, or painful mistakes on both sides.
Those things deserve honest examination.
Repentance may be needed. Counseling may be needed. Difficult conversations may be needed.
But marital imperfection does not make adultery righteous.
And your failures, whatever they may be, do not give another person permission to use God's name to justify wrongdoing.
You do not have to compete with a third person to prove that your covenant mattered.
You do not have to become someone else's fantasy to earn basic faithfulness.
You do not have to accept a spiritually intimidating statement as the final word over your life.
You can say, calmly and firmly:

“I cannot accept that God has instructed you to pursue another marriage in violation of His Word. I am willing to seek truth, repentance, and wise counsel. But I will not call betrayal obedience to God.”
That is not rebellion against the Lord.
That is a refusal to confuse the Lord's authority with another person's claim to possess it.
And please understand something else.
Biblical forgiveness does not require you to pretend that nothing happened.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical.
Forgiveness involves releasing personal vengeance and entrusting justice to God.
Reconciliation involves rebuilding a relationship where truth, repentance, safety, and trust matter.
If a spouse has been unfaithful, meaningful restoration cannot be built on denial.
There must be honesty.
The outside relationship must end.
Deception must be confronted.
Accountability must be welcomed.
And rebuilding trust may take a long time.
Luke 17:3 teaches the seriousness of rebuke, repentance, and forgiveness. Ephesians 4:25 calls believers to put away falsehood and speak truthfully.
None of this means a wounded spouse must immediately restore access, intimacy, or trust simply because the offending spouse says, “I've repented.”
Words matter.
But patterns of conduct matter too.
And if there is abuse, intimidation, coercion, threats, or danger, seeking safety is not a betrayal of marriage.
Please do not let anyone use the language of submission, forgiveness, or covenant to pressure you into remaining in an unsafe situation.
Find trusted support. Seek qualified professional and pastoral help. In immediate danger, prioritize safety and contact appropriate emergency services.
The God who commands faithfulness does not authorize cruelty.
But perhaps another question is burning inside you.
“Does this mean I must remain married no matter what happens?”
We need to be careful here because people have been deeply harmed by simplistic answers to complicated biblical questions.
Jesus speaks about sexual immorality and divorce in Matthew 19:9. Paul addresses marriage, separation, and abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7:10–15.
Faithful Christians differ in how they interpret the precise grounds for divorce and remarriage, especially in complex situations involving abuse, desertion, and questions of repentance.
Those differences should not be erased by pretending every case has an identical answer.
But the biblical passages do not establish a general permission to discard a spouse merely because someone claims God has chosen a new romantic partner.
And the person who has been betrayed should not be forced into an immediate decision about divorce, reconciliation, or remarriage while still in shock.
Seek wise counsel from people who understand Scripture, respect your safety, and will not manipulate you into protecting appearances at the expense of truth.
Proverbs 15:22 teaches the value of wise counsel.
That counsel should be careful, accountable, and willing to hear the full situation rather than simply siding with whichever spouse speaks more confidently about hearing God's voice.
And now we must talk about something the church sometimes gets terribly wrong.
There are believers who are more concerned about saving the image of a marriage than protecting the people suffering inside it.
They tell the wounded spouse to smile.
Pray harder.
Submit more.
Stop talking about what happened.
Protect the ministry.
Protect the family's reputation.
And somehow, the person who has been betrayed ends up carrying the shame of the person who committed the betrayal.
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus never taught that protecting a religious image is more important than walking in truth.
He exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted sin.
He welcomed the brokenhearted.
He called sinners to repentance.
And He offered grace that transforms people rather than merely helping them conceal their behavior.
Remember the woman caught in adultery in John 8.

The passage has a well-known textual history: the account in John 7:53–8:11 is absent from many of the earliest Greek manuscripts and appears in different locations in some manuscript traditions. It should therefore be handled with appropriate textual care rather than used as the sole foundation for a doctrine.
Yet the scene, as traditionally received in Christian Scripture, captures two truths Christians must never separate.
Jesus refused to let the woman's accusers turn her into an object of merciless condemnation.
And He also said:
“Go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Grace did not mean adultery was suddenly acceptable.
Mercy did not mean repentance was unnecessary.
The woman was not told that her past made her beyond redemption.
But neither was she told to rename her sin as God's will.
That is the tension we must preserve.
Jesus is merciful enough to receive sinners and holy enough to call them away from sin.
And if you are the spouse who has developed feelings for someone else, I want to speak to you too.
Not to humiliate you.
Not to declare that your life is beyond hope.
But because your soul matters too much for someone to flatter you into spiritual danger.
Maybe your marriage has become lonely.
Maybe you feel unseen.
Maybe another person listens to you in ways your spouse hasn't for years.
Maybe you have been telling yourself that such a deep emotional connection must have been arranged by God.
But before you call it destiny, examine it in the light of Scripture.
Have you been hiding conversations?
Have you crossed boundaries you would be ashamed for your spouse to discover?
Have you compared your spouse's worst moments with someone else's most attractive qualities?
Have you used prayer to justify what honesty would expose?
And have you considered the pain your choices may bring to children, families, and the person who once trusted you with their heart?
If the answer exposes sin, do not despair.
But do not disguise it either.
Repentance begins where self-justification ends.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) is commonly translated “repentance.” It conveys a change of mind or heart that, in biblical usage, is bound up with turning toward God and away from sin.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible after being caught.
It is not crying because a relationship became complicated.
It is not saying “God knows my heart” while continuing the behavior you refuse to surrender.
Genuine repentance turns toward the truth.
First John 1:9 offers this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise is beautiful.
But notice that it speaks of confessing sin—not renaming it.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than a moral warning.
Because the central message of Christianity is not that good people never make devastating mistakes.
The Gospel is that sinners need a Savior.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for our sins and rose again, as proclaimed in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
He did not go to the cross to make betrayal respectable.
He went to the cross to save sinners and reconcile us to God.
His grace is not permission to continue in darkness.
It is the power and invitation to come into the light.
The cross tells the guilty that forgiveness is possible.
And it tells the wounded that evil does not have the final word.
Perhaps your spouse will repent.
Perhaps your marriage will be rebuilt slowly, with tears, accountability, prayer, and years of renewed faithfulness.
Perhaps the restoration you long for will not happen.
Perhaps the other person will continue insisting that God has spoken, even when Scripture confronts the claim.
I cannot promise you that your spouse will return.
I cannot promise that every broken marriage will be restored.
And I will not insult your pain by pretending that a Bible verse can erase betrayal overnight.
But I can tell you what the Gospel promises to those who belong to Christ.
Your hope is not ultimately held in the hands of the person who hurt you.
Psalm 34:18 declares:
“The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.” (KJV)
That does not mean you will stop hurting tomorrow.
It means your heartbreak does not place you beyond God's compassion.
You may still need counseling.
You may need to establish boundaries.
You may need legal guidance.
You may need to protect your children from adult conflict.
You may need to grieve a future you thought was certain.
And through all of it, you can still belong to Jesus.
Even if your spouse chooses someone else.
Even if people misunderstand your story.
Even if your prayers are answered differently from what you desperately hoped.
Your identity in Christ is not cancelled by another person's unfaithfulness.
And that is why I want you to remember a particular scene from Scripture.
After Peter denied Jesus three times, he carried the terrible knowledge that he had failed the One he loved.
Yet in John 21, the risen Christ met Peter again.
Jesus did not pretend the denial never happened.
He confronted Peter with questions of love and entrusted him with renewed responsibility.
Peter's restoration was not proof that sin had been harmless.
It was proof that failure need not be the final chapter for a repentant disciple.
Now, Peter's denial was not marital adultery, and his restoration should never be used to pressure a betrayed spouse into immediate reconciliation.
But the scene reveals something essential about Jesus.
He does not merely expose what is broken.
He is able to restore those who truly turn to Him.
And that brings us to the heart of everything Gospel Warrior stands for.
Not because scandal is secretly good.
Not because every betrayal leads to a restored marriage.
Not because God approves of what people do in His name.
But because Jesus Christ can bring forgiveness, holiness, healing, and new life into stories that human beings have damaged.
Sometimes grace looks like a marriage being rebuilt.
Sometimes it looks like a betrayed person learning to stand again.
Sometimes it looks like a guilty person finally confessing without excuses.
Sometimes it looks like finding the courage to leave a dangerous situation.
Sometimes it looks like a long season of grief in which God is teaching someone that their worth was never dependent on being chosen by another human being.
The circumstances may differ.
But Jesus remains the center.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, perhaps this is the prayer you have been unable to put into words:

“Lord Jesus, I do not understand why this is happening. I feel rejected, confused, and afraid. Please keep bitterness from destroying my heart. Give me discernment to recognize truth, courage to establish righteous boundaries, humility to acknowledge my own sins, and wisdom to seek help. If restoration is possible, let it be built on genuine repentance and truth. If it is not, hold me close as I grieve. Do not let another person's choices pull me away from You. Teach me to trust Your character even when I cannot understand my circumstances. In Your name, amen.”
Maybe that prayer is yours.
Maybe it belongs to someone you know.
And maybe, as you read this, you realize that the most urgent question is no longer, “How do I make my spouse choose me?”
Maybe it has become:
“How do I remain faithful to Jesus when someone I trusted has broken my heart?”
That is a question worth bringing into the light.
If you have experienced God's sustaining grace after betrayal, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may help someone who feels completely alone.
You do not need to reveal private details, identify another person, or disclose anything that could put you or your children at risk.
But please remember: a comment section is not a substitute for trusted, confidential support.

And if someone comes to mind while you read this—perhaps a friend who is struggling with marital betrayal, a believer confused about God's will, or someone who has mistaken romantic excitement for divine direction—consider sharing this article with them privately.
Not to shame a particular spouse.
Not to turn someone's private suffering into public entertainment.
But to help more people understand that biblical love, covenant faithfulness, repentance, and grace must never be separated.
We want this community to be a place where people can ask difficult questions without being shamed for having them—and where the answers continually lead us back to Jesus Christ.
Not because you can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because financial support replaces repentance, prayer, generosity to your local church, or obedience to God's Word.
Giving is to be voluntary, thoughtful, and free from coercion, consistent with the principle of 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But the deepest value we hope to offer is not merchandise.
It is continued encouragement to know Christ more deeply, study His Word faithfully, and grow in a community that takes both grace and truth seriously.
Because the purpose of Gospel Warrior is not to build a following around human personalities.
It is to point people toward the Savior who died and rose again.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the person sitting across from a spouse who has just said:
“God told me to marry someone else.”
You may not be able to control what happens next.
You cannot force another person to repent.
You cannot make someone honor vows they are determined to break.
You cannot heal a marriage through your faithfulness alone when the other person refuses truth and accountability.
But you can refuse to believe that the God revealed in Jesus Christ has abandoned you simply because another human being has invoked His name.
You can open your Bible.
You can seek wise and safe counsel.
You can grieve without surrendering your dignity.
You can repent of your own sins without accepting responsibility for someone else's.
You can forgive without pretending that trust has already been restored.
And you can entrust your future to the Lord without pretending you know exactly how the story will unfold.
Because the Gospel does not promise that every person who leaves will return.
It promises that everyone who comes to Jesus Christ in genuine faith and repentance will find a Savior who is able to forgive, redeem, and make all things new.
And perhaps that is what someone desperately needs to hear tonight.
The person who broke your heart may have changed their mind about you.
But their decision does not change the character of Jesus.
Their words are not Scripture.
Their desires are not divine decrees.
And their departure does not have the authority to erase your worth as someone made in the image of God.
The person who promised you forever may have walked away, but the Savior who gave His life for you has not stopped calling you to Himself.
